p.s: Replicating and remixing proven competitor ads

p.t:
Copy the **structure** of a winning ad, never its exact words, look or footage.
Change at least **one element** before you use a competitor's idea.
Test every idea yourself. Keep it only if its **click and result numbers** reach your goals.
Save **20 top videos per product on Kalodata, or 3 to 5 top ads** on TikTok Creative Center or Facebook Ad Library.
**Copy the structure** of a proven ad, then change the words, reviews and brand details.
**Change one key element** of a copied ad, such as the hook, before use. Exception: the first launch of a ripped ad.
**Change the metadata** (hidden file details) of every copied ad, so platforms do not see duplicates.
**Test with a small budget** first, then check purchases and ROAS before you spend more.
Core rule: copy the structure, never the words
p.s: Replicating and remixing proven competitor ads

p.t: Do **not copy** competitor ad creatives straight from the Meta Ad Library (Meta's public list of running ads) without changes.
Meta (the company that runs Facebook and Instagram) gives preference to the competitor's established account history, so direct copies do not get equal reach.
When you use a competitor creative (their ad video or image) as a reference, **edit at least one element**.
Choose the hook (the first seconds that catch attention), the body copy (the main written text), or something else that makes your version different.
Imitation means **learning** from structure and form, not copying word for word. The line between plagiarism (copying someone else's work) and genius is fine.
Imitation is a logical learning step before innovation (new ideas). Great poets imitate and improve; small poets steal and spoil.

Competitor ads are the best **starting point** for your own creative (the video or image you run). If they cannot be used, build your own ad from competitor content and improve it rather than copying it.
A competitor ad works best as a structure to follow, not a look to copy. **Reuse the arrangement** of headline, product and offer.
Take colours, fonts (letter styles) and brand identity (the look and feel of a brand) from your own brand. This keeps the test about the structure and avoids using another brand's identity.

Look for patterns across several videos, such as a hook or ad copy used again and again. **Replicate the pattern with your own footage (raw video you shot or recorded). Do not copy a brand's custom content.**
**For drop-shipping style videos (ads for products you sell without holding stock, called dropshipping), produce a better version** or rearrange existing clips.

Use a competitor's idea as a starting point only if you test it yourself. **Keep it only if** click numbers (CTR, click-through rate: the share of viewers who click the ad) and result numbers reach your targets.
Otherwise change the creative or the offer.

Copying other dropshippers' creatives is acceptable at the very beginning. In the long run, your own creatives perform better. **Order the product and film your own material.** This usually beats reusing other ads.
Core rule: copy the structure, never the words (continued)
p.s: Replicating and remixing proven competitor ads

p.t: Use a proven line from your **Structure Library (a saved collection) and its Proven Line-Patterns (lines that already worked) as an example of a psychological move (a way of making people feel or act).**

**Do not use it as a phrase to repeat. Default to reproducing the move with fresh words**. Use a proven line word for word only if it is genuinely the strongest option, never to avoid the work of writing a fresh version.

Competitor creatives can serve as inspiration. Take their images or GIFs (short looping animated pictures), edit them, and **improve headlines (the big title text) and angles (the main idea of the ad) with editing tools.**
**Do not use them unchanged. The aim is a clearly better version** than the competitor's ad or landing page (the page people reach after clicking).
Recreate a viral competitor video (one that spread widely) by **improving its hook** or other weak parts, not by copying it.
Repurpose existing competitor footage by cutting out their text and logos, changing the brand colours and adding a **new narrative** (a new story).
The goal is a different story built on the same footage, not a copy of the original ad.
Exact copy-paste is risky. The platform can detect it. The competitor may get the original ad taken down, which takes your ad down too.
**Always alter** the metadata (hidden details such as file name and tags), the logo and the details of any replicated creative.
Copying a competitor's ads and store exactly can produce high CPM (cost per 1,000 views) and poor CTR (click-through rate). **Change elements** such as music, speed, length and hook.
This stops Meta from treating them as duplicates (copies) of another advertiser's content.
Instead of reusing a brand's ad video, **copy its hook or structure**. Find your own clips on AliExpress, Alibaba or YouTube (online shopping and video sites).
This keeps the selling pattern, avoids the brand's content and reduces copyright risk (the chance of legal trouble over someone else's work).
Sourcing proven creatives: Where to look and what to save
p.s: Replicating and remixing proven competitor ads

p.t: Ripped creatives are videos that already perform for other advertisers.
Find them on **Kalodata (a tool that tracks ads and products), the TikTok Creative Center (TikTok's free ad library) or the Facebook Ad Library (Meta's public list of running ads).**
**Their audience psychology is already proven, which makes them a safe first test**.

Ad libraries show what creative types work, including posts that go viral. Identify which trends, post types and ad types work. Then **recreate the winning approach** in your own style without copying it.
Pool-building (collecting a large set of options): Kalodata lists **more than 4,000** video and ad creatives for one product.
Use that pool to pull hooks and testimonials (customer stories on video) and build many variations, not one or two new ads.

Content from other products in the **same category** can serve your product. Eyeliner ads, for example, can supply hooks and testimonials for another eyeliner. This widens your pool well beyond one product's ads.
Do not run the same top-performing competitor ads that many advertisers already show on Facebook. The audience has probably seen them.
**Bring content** the market has not seen yet, even when the product is the same.
Choose only videos that feature **real people**. Abstract videos and product-only videos are excluded.
In the table below, **spend means the money spent on an ad. Conversions means sales. Engagement** means likes, comments and shares.

For every saved video, **also save** its caption (the written text under the post), text overlays (words shown on screen), hook and call to action (CTA: the line or button that asks the viewer to act).
These are the basis for later comparison.
Download only **clean versions** without a watermark (a logo or name placed on the video). A watermark shows another account's branding inside your ad.

p.t: Judge each candidate on two checks. The opening hook must grab attention. The video must show a problem your product actually solves.
A video can pass the hook check and still fail the second one, so **both checks are needed**.
**Skip a video** if the outcome it shows is not the result your product delivers, even when the hook performs well.
**Filter for high CTR and proven conversions** before you test a video in your own account. Recycling earlier ads with the same structure also saves production time (the time spent making an ad).

Break each successful competitor creative down **every five seconds** to identify the hook, the angle (main idea)

Study the competitor's ad for the same product. Save the videos, review what worked, and **copy the structure**, text-to-speech (a computer voice that reads text aloud) and sounds in your own way.
This is often more effective than writing a script (the written plan of spoken words) from scratch.
Copy the style of the largest pages or videos for your product. Then change it based on what viewers say in the comments, and **add something dramatic or unusual**.
Changes that work include new trending sounds, different backdrops (background scenes), switching between a male and a female presenter, trending video effects,
voice-overs (spoken narration added over the video) and challenge-style framing (a format where the person takes on a challenge).

p.h: Prompts for analysis and recreation: Analysis prompt for a proven rival video

p.t: Here is a proven rival video, sent along with its video file and the brand data I exported. Give me a complete breakdown of why it wins.
Go through it frame by frame, and for each moment describe what appears on screen, what is spoken, and what effect that has on the viewer.
Give special weight to the hook in the opening seconds and to the individual words and phrases doing the heaviest persuasive work, explaining per frame why each one lands.
Using the supplied brand data, identify the persona, the core desire, the emotions in play, the awareness level, the concept, the angle, the USPs, and the offer behind the video.
End with a brief list of what to keep and what to modify if this same structure is applied to a different product.
(Send it with the video file, the brand data and your product files.)

p.t: Here is the winning video from my competitor and its exported brand data.

Replace only the product, its facts, prices, ingredients and claims with those of my product, using only the facts in the attached product files and inventing no new claims.
Output the full script for my product, scene by scene.

Testing ripped videos unchanged isolates whether the product and offer work, because the videos have already been proven with real viewers.
Changing the hook, caption or length of a ripped video before the first launch removes the advantage of testing a proven ad. The result no longer shows whether the original works.
Case: a seller (an operator) sold a product using only ripped creatives, with no original content. The proven videos were downloaded without watermark and uploaded unchanged to the ad account.

Hook from one ad, testimonial from another
p.s: Replicating and remixing proven competitor ads

p.t: Case and method: a NAD+ (a health supplement) berry drink mix was running top ads on Meta and TikTok.
The leading ad was shown with a figure of 27k.
Several competitors the speaker knew personally were running the same ads. Running them again would reach a **saturated audience** (people who have already seen the ads too often).
The seller searched Kalodata. The seller found the same NAD+ product in drops form (liquid drops) with its own set of video ads.
The seller saved a hook from one of those ads, which showed a benefit for looking younger.
In CapCut (a video editing app), the seller cut the hook off after it ended.
The seller combined it with a testimonial from another ad, in which an older parent looked young because of the product, and produced a new creative.
The seller reported that this method produced the first winning ad from the first winning product. Kalodata listed **over 4,000 creatives** per product to repeat the process.
1. In Kalodata, set the **region (country) to United States and the period to Last 30 Days**. Choose a product that is already advertised.
2. **Do not use** the top-performing ad itself. Look for the same product in another form (for example, drink mix versus drops) that has its own video ads.
3. Open that product's **Video & Ad list** (Kalodata's list of videos for a product).
Watch the videos until you find a strong hook, meaning the opening seconds that stop the scroll (make people pause as they scroll past).
4. Save the video by downloading it **without watermark**, keeping the plan download limit (how many downloads your plan allows) in mind.
5. Import the clip into CapCut using **Stay in original location** (a CapCut import option that keeps the file where it is).
6. **Cut the clip right after the hook ends.** Do not keep the full video.
7. Find a testimonial clip, where a person describes a result, from another ad for the same product or from the same category.
8. **Combine the hook and the testimonial** into one new creative.

When copying a winning ad, **change the hook**, the first image or the first seconds so the ad is unique. The more different the creative, the better. An identical copy is the lazy option.

Only then produce unique videos or go to creators or influencers (people with large social audiences who promote products).

**Improvement cycle for a winning creative**
1. In Ads Manager (the tool to run and track ads on Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram), **identify** the creative with the most website purchases (sales made on your site after an ad click).
2. **Convert** the winner to text in Google AI Studio (Gemini), capturing both the primary text and the headline.
3. **Rebuild** the messaging with Claude. Define the angle (the main point you push), the promise (what the buyer gets) and the objection (the doubt the buyer has) it addresses.
4. **Adapt** the winning message into new formats: podcast, conference, seminar, claymation (clay animation), cartoon and UGC AI ads.
UGC means user-generated content, videos that look made by real customers or creators.
5. **Run a 3-day launch test** in a testing CBO (campaign budget optimization, where the platform splits one budget across your ads).
Evaluate website purchases and ROAS (return on ad spend, the money earned for each unit spent on ads).
Take the best-performing creative (the one with the best results). Pass it through the transcribe-and-rebuild cycle. **Release two new formats** that carry the same message.
What to change and what to keep
p.s: Replicating and remixing proven competitor ads

p.t:
**Elements and rules**
**Hook (the first seconds that stop people scrolling)**

What to do: Keep it when copying a winner. Change it only when the copy must be unique, or as a later test once a product sells consistently.
**Video length**

What to do: Keep it in the first launch of ripped creatives (ads copied from others).
**Caption**

What to do: Keep the text. If you cover original captions, use the same text on top. Change caption colour if needed.
**Music**

What to do: Keep the original music unless you are testing. Changing it can break a working creative (make a good ad stop working).
**Speed and clip order**

What to do: Alter (change) after about 7 to 10 seconds, or after the first 3 to 5 seconds. Do not alter the hook.
**Logo**

What to do: Replace or cover the competitor logo. Add your own at the top of the frame (the screen area).
**Metadata (hidden file details, such as title and tags)**

What to do: Always alter it for a replicated creative.
**Personal details**

What to do: Remove mentions of TikTok Shop or Orange Cart. TikTok is a short-video app. These are names of sales tools.
**Product claims (statements about what the product does)**

What to do: Replace only product facts, prices, ingredients and claims. Invent no new claims.
**Messaging**

What to do: Keep the structure. Rewrite the words.
Note: the messaging row cites and for structure-only rewriting. Use the framework above as the reference.

**Where sources disagree**
**Change a competitor's creative before use?**

Advice A: Change at least one element: the hook, the body copy (main text) or another differentiator (what makes you different). Do not copy directly from the Ad Library (Meta's public list of running ads).
Advice B: Keep a ripped video unchanged in the first launch. Test what already works.
When each applies: Change competitor creatives you reuse as reference or as copies. Keep ripped creatives unchanged only for the first launch.
What to change and what to keep (continued)
p.s: Replicating and remixing proven competitor ads

p.t:
Before that, remove watermarks (logos or text stamped on the video) and TikTok Shop or Orange Cart mentions.
**Edit the hook?**
Advice A: Keep the hook of a winning competitor video closely. Keep the hook unchanged for proven videos. Remove only problematic parts.
Advice B: Change the hook, the first image or the first seconds so the ad is unique. Hook-only tests are a valid method.
When each applies: Keep the hook for copies and first launches. Change the hook for unique creatives, or as a single-variable test (changing only one thing) on a proven ad.

Start hook testing once the ripped creative sells consistently.
**Music and speed**
Advice A: Change music, speed, length or hook so Meta does not see duplicates (copies it flags as the same ad). Change the speed and the metadata.
Advice B: Keep music. A changed music track flopped (failed badly) in one copy.
When each applies: Change speed and metadata to avoid duplicate detection. Keep the music unless you are testing a music change on its own.
**Reuse an old or still-running video?**
Advice A: On Facebook, small changes such as a new logo or caption lower the risk of higher CPM (cost per 1,000 views).
Export a changed aspect ratio (the shape of the frame) or caption as a new file before reuse.
Advice B: On TikTok, reusing an old creative is more likely to raise CPM and lower CTR (click-through rate, the share of viewers who click).

When each applies: Facebook: apply visible changes and re-export (save again as a new file). TikTok: prefer a new creative over an old one.
**Exact copy running badly?**
Advice A: Close the campaign (the group of ads) and duplicate it to reset delivery (how the platform shows the ad). One case with no sales for four days recovered to about three sales in a day.
Advice B: Send the product to a UGC creator for original content with the same strategy.
What to change and what to keep (continued)
p.s: Replicating and remixing proven competitor ads

p.t: When each applies: Reset first if delivery metrics (the numbers showing how the ad reaches people) are poor but the creative is sound. Commission (pay for) original content if the copy keeps underperforming.

**Imitation or originality?**
Advice A: Copy the structure and sell with a proven pattern.
Advice B: Dropshipping (selling products you do not stock, with the supplier shipping them) copies are acceptable at the start. Own creatives perform better long-term.

When each applies: Copy structure at the start. Move to your own footage (your own videos) once the product shows traction (clear signs of sales).
**Replace borrowed footage**
**Replace** borrowed footage with your own UGC once the product shows traction.

Once a product shows good performance, **invest in custom content** (made-to-order videos or pictures) for it.
**Selection and fit**
A strong hook alone is not enough. **Check** that the outcome the video shows matches what your product delivers.

**Test design**
**Test the new version** with a controlled budget (a fixed, small amount of spend) before scaling.

Testing a winning competitor ad:
1. **Pick** the competitor ad that is scaling (its spend and sales are growing).
2. **Copy the hook** exactly.
3. **Edit** the later part of the video (clips or pacing, the speed of the cuts).
4. **Change the metadata** (for example video speed or clip layout) with a metadata-editing tool (a tool that changes hidden file details), so the ad is not identical.
5. **Test** the new version with a controlled budget before scaling.
**Keep** a competitor's idea only if the click and result numbers reach your targets. Otherwise change the creative or the offer (the deal, price or bonus).

Testing competitor creatives for a new product:
1. **Download** the videos competitors run.

2. **Upload** them to your Business Manager (Meta's tool for managing ad accounts and assets).
3. **Test** their performance for your product.
Testing copies (continued)
p.s: Replicating and remixing proven competitor ads

p.t:
4. **Produce** your own edited version once you see results.
**Rotate** new mashups (versions that blend parts of other ads) when a version stops performing.
**Run a 3-day launch test** in a testing CBO and evaluate website purchases and ROAS.
Ripped creatives: **start with unchanged videos** for the product and offer test. Then begin hook testing to raise CTR once profitable sales (sales that make money) are steady.

**Test order**
1. **Start with** existing high-performing videos from the market. Edit the first three seconds to find the best CTR.
2. **Only then** produce unique videos or work with creators or influencers.
3. **Reuse** existing videos to test several products at once. Invest in custom content for products that perform.
A German acupuncture pen store launched by **copying a US competitor's product page and ad feed (the list of ads a brand runs) in full.**
**With a EUR 50 test, the first day brought five sales. The product scaled to about EUR 5,000 to 6,000 per day** at roughly 30 percent margin (the share of each sale kept as profit).
Sales dropped later as the creatives wore out (stopped working). New creatives were sourced from a freelancer (a hired person paid per job) to replace them.
A ripped-creative operator sold a product with no original content. The operator reported **more than 16,000 USD** in revenue (total sales money) in one day from ripped ads alone.
The NAD+ hook-and-testimonial remix (a re-edit combining a hook with a testimonial, a customer review video) described above produced the **first winning ad** from the first winning product.
A ripped copy sent to a drop-shipping style test: a copied competitor page and ad feed, with the EUR 50 test above, **followed the same path** as the acupuncture case.
Wordtune (an AI writing tool) can **rewrite** copied competitor landing-page text into your own wording while keeping the same benefits.
Use it after you have collected the competitor copy and checked which benefits it states.
